p: kufta, which is an acronym for kuf vetiv, which means turn it over and sit. Bricks are called livnei,
hutza and Rav Yehuda said that it is merely a ḥatzitza,
ḥatzba because it hews [ḥotzev] water from the river. … kuza, … kazeh, … shutita, … shetuta, … meshikhla, … mashei kula, … mashkhilta,

ḥatzba because it hews [ḥotzev] water from the river. A small jug is called kuza, alluding to kazeh, which means: Give me one like that. Myrtle branches with which people dance at a wedding are called shutita, an allusion to shetuta, which means madness, as the frenzied dancing appears to be madness. The large vessel used for washing is called meshikhla, which is an acronym for mashei kula, which means: It washes all. A small vessel used for washing is called mashkhilta,
mashya kalta, which means: It washes the bride. A mortar is called asita,
ḥasirta, which means lacking, since it has a large cavity. The pestle that is inserted into the mortar for pounding its contents is called bukhna,
levusha, which is an acronym for lo busha, which means no shame, as one who is clothed is no longer ashamed. A broad outer garment is called gelima,
purya, an allusion to the fact that people parin veravin,
bor zinka, which is an acronym for bor ze naki, which means that this pit is empty of water. The head covering of Torah scholars is called sudara,
“The counsel of the Lord is with them who fear Him [sod Hashem lire’av]” … apadna, … apitḥa dein,
